19.0.0.en: "Beyond Jordan": it is the region lying beside the river Jordan, called Perea, and anciently the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh dwelt in it, and it is now called the Golan.

19.0.1.en: After His teachings that Matthew the Evangelist mentioned in the previous chapter, Christ left the region of Galilee, which lies in the north, where He had spent about three years, and moved to Judea, which is the southern region and contains Jerusalem, passing by the river Jordan, and He did not head quickly to Jerusalem, but moved about quietly in this region before reaching it.

19.0.2.en: Christ spent in this journey, from Galilee to Jerusalem, a period of about six months, during which many things happened that Luke and John mentioned, whereas Matthew mentioned a few events of them in this chapter and the one after it.

19.0.3.en: And Matthew mentioned that great multitudes followed Him, and He taught them His spiritual teachings and healed their sick as was His custom.

19.1.0.en: Here is clear teaching about the sacrament of marriage, which Christ established by His presence at the wedding at Cana of Galilee at the beginning of His ministry. The motive for it was the Pharisees' question to Him about the permitted reasons for a man to divorce his wife: for any cause, or are there specific causes? They knew, from His Sermon on the Mount, His opinion that divorce is not permitted except for the cause of adultery (ch. 5:32). Therefore, this question of theirs was not to know the truth, but to catch Him in a word, because if He forbade divorce He would be regarded as breaking the law of Moses which permits it (Deut 24:1 and 3), and to stir up Herod against Him because he had divorced his wife and married Herodias.

19.1.1.en: And Christ cited the words of Moses in the Torah, and took them back to the beginning of creation, when God created Eve from the side of Adam, and Adam declared in the spirit of prophecy that when a man marries, he should leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, "and they twain shall be one flesh" (Gen 2:24), and so God joined them together in the sacrament of marriage, so how can we permit the separation of what God has joined?!

19.1.2.en: So divorce is a breaking of what God has done, and it is against it.

19.2.0.en: The Pharisees objected to the words of Christ, that Moses permitted divorce, so how does He forbid it?!

19.2.1.en: Christ replied to them that this permission was because of their low spiritual level, because after their mixing with the Egyptians they had become accustomed to divorce. So when they went out into the wilderness, He moved them gradually to the original law by narrowing the possibility of divorce, so that they would afterward leave it entirely, since the natural, sound state that God established in the Garden of Eden between Adam and Eve was the union of the two and the non-permission of divorce.

19.2.2.en: And Moses did not command divorce, but on the contrary, he commanded the one who wishes to divorce his wife not to be hasty, but to sit down and write her a bill of divorcement, to give him an opportunity to review himself and let his anger subside, so that he would reverse his decision if he thought that his wife would be with another, and that he would demolish his house and scatter his children.

19.3.0.en: After Christ's conversation with the Pharisees ended, He entered a house, as our teacher Mark mentions (Mk 10:10), and continued His talk with His disciples, affirming the law of the New Testament, which is that the only reason permitted for divorce in Christianity is the fall of one of the two parties into adultery, for by this he has separated bodily from the other, so the divorce has actually taken place bodily, and the writing of a bill of divorce is permitted.

19.3.1.en: But as for the one who wants to divorce his wife because of disagreements between them, the Church does not approve of that, for he is united with her in the sight of God.

19.3.2.en: But if this person resorts to trickery and obtains a civil divorce that the Church does not recognize and marries another, he falls into adultery. And whoever marries a woman divorced for a cause other than adultery, both of them fall into adultery.

19.3.3.en: The existence of differences in opinions and characters is not solved by divorce, but by taking refuge in God so that a person gives up some of his characteristics. By this he not only restores peace in his home, but his will also grows, so he is able to advance spiritually and control his desires and sins; and thus the affliction turns into a blessing, that is, the problems of marriage become a means of spiritual growth.

19.4.0.en: Since Christ did not permit divorce except for adultery, the hearers felt that this was beyond human endurance, and that it is better not to marry, because they did not understand the greatness of the oneness between the spouses, for divorce for any disagreements was easy in their view, and they were not ready to bear with one another.

19.5.0.en: Christ seized this opportunity to explain the difference between not marrying (celibacy) and virginity, and showed that there are three kinds of unmarried people:

19.5.1.en: The first kind: one who was born with sexual impotence, so he cannot marry, not out of love for virginity and being with God, but because of his inability to do so.

19.5.2.en: The second kind: those who wanted to serve in the palaces of the great and the kings, so they had an operation of removal performed on them, and became sexually impotent, in order to obtain a position or work in these palaces, where they would be trusted with serving the women without fear of assault on them. His not marrying in this case is for the sake of the desire for position and money, and to please people, and this is the worst kind.

19.5.3.en: The third kind: those who have risen above and sublimated the sexual instinct, and turned it into energy for the love of God, so that, although they are physically able to marry, they have turned their thought and their heart to the love of God as a heavenly Bridegroom, so they are in a spiritual marriage with God, higher than every human marriage.

19.5.4.en: This is virginity, whether serving in the world or in monasticism, and it is for some people to whom God has granted this grace and the inclination to be content with it, and not everyone can receive it, but it is very great if a person is fit for it.

19.5.5.en: "He that is able to receive it, let him receive it": that is, whoever has an inclination to virginity, it is good for him to live by it, and so enjoy the consecration of his thought and his heart to God.

19.5.6.en: If you are not fit for virginity, then at least be chaste from sin before marriage. And even after marriage, let your chief concern not be absorption in the bodily relationship to the point of disagreeing with your life partner, but give a greater place to the love of God in your heart, and to love of the other and appreciation of his feelings, so that you give up thinking about this relationship in order to please the other, or enter into this relationship, even if you are not inclined to it, also in order to please the other; do not seek your comfort but his, for this is true love.

19.6.0.en: Christ was blessing and healing the sick, and caring for teaching and solving people's problems. So some fathers brought their children to Him that He might pray over them and bless them.

19.6.1.en: But the disciples felt that their Teacher's time was too precious to waste on caring for children, so they tried to keep them away from Him so that He might attend to the affairs of adults.

19.7.0.en: Christ was not content with blessing the children and welcoming them, but declared an important truth, which is that these children are the children of the heavenly Kingdom, calling us all to imitate their innocence and simplicity. And although the child was neglected at that time in the prevailing religions, and in the earlier ages and kingdoms, Christianity cares for children, and even calls adults to learn from them, and to care for them and look after them.

19.7.1.en: "Of such": that is, of those who imitate them in innocence and simplicity.

19.8.0.en: A rich young man came to Christ (v. 22), and he was a ruler of one of the synagogues of the Jews (Lk 18:

19.8.1.en: 18), and since he was accustomed to flowery speech, he called Christ Good Master, and asked Him a spiritual question, which was how to attain eternal life. Christ was concerned with his question, but before answering him, He directed his attention to not using words of praise without understanding, so He said to him: "Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God." And the meaning of the question: do you believe that I am God, or do you say it as a mere compliment? And Christ is of course the Good Teacher, indeed the Good Shepherd as He said of Himself (Jn 10:11), and He is God without sin, as He said to the Jews: "Which of you convinceth me of sin?" (Jn 8:46). Then He answered the question that the way to eternity is keeping the commandments and carrying them out in life.

19.9.0.en: The young man asked Christ: "Which?" And Christ answered: "All the commandments that are on the two tablets that Moses received from God, whether those concerning the worship of God or dealing with others."

19.9.1.en: And Christ focused on the commandments of the second tablet, which concern dealing with others, because they cannot be fulfilled except by keeping the commandments of the first tablet, which are the worship of God and His love.

19.9.2.en: And Christ summed up at the end of His reply the commandments of the second tablet by saying: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."

19.10.0.en: The young man answered hastily that he had kept these commandments from his youth. But Christ's intention was not keeping them literally, or applying them superficially, but with all their depths. Therefore Christ focused on treating the disease within him, so that he would understand the depth of applying the commandment, for his problem is the love of money, and He told him that he lacks one thing, that is, the treatment of the love of money (Mk 10:21).

19.11.0.en: Christ asked the young man to sell his possessions and distribute the price to the poor, and by this he would transfer his treasure from earth to heaven and his heart would be attached to it. And as an extension of this thought, he would follow Christ to walk in His teachings. † The actual application of these commandments is Christian perfection, and if a person cannot apply these words literally, as Anba Anthony the father of monks did, he should at least sell the love of material things from his heart, that is, be ready to give them up, and partly leave these possessions and give them to the needy.

19.12.0.en: Before the clear words of Christ, the weakness of this young man and his love of money were exposed, for he went away sorrowful, since he could not carry out the words of Christ, because his love of money was stronger than his love of God, and his great wealth helped his heart to cling to the love of money.

19.12.1.en: To be a child of the Kingdom, you must love God more than you love material things, and the proof of this is your offering of the firstfruits and the tithes however tight your financial circumstances, and that you be ready to give up material things to please those around you, and be content with everything.

19.13.0.en: Christ commented to His disciples on His dialogue with the young man after he left, explaining the danger of the love of money, and said that it is very hard for a rich man, who loves his wealth and relies on it, to enter the Kingdom of Heaven. And He likened that to a huge camel passing through the eye of a needle, and this is impossible, so likewise the rich man cannot enter the Kingdom. So he must first sell from his heart the love of money and reliance on it, and even if he has much money, it does not hinder him from entering the Kingdom because his heart is not in it.

19.14.0.en: The disciples felt the difficulty of carrying out these words, because their thinking was attached to the earthly kingship of Christ and the love of wealth and position, so Christ directed their gaze to the help of God which helps a person to do this, for what seems impossible in the eyes of man becomes easy with the help of God.

19.14.1.en: And this is what actually happened in the lives of many rich saints, who left their wealth and possessions, and lived in poverty in monastic life, or came forward to torture and martyrdom for the sake of Christ.

19.14.2.en: If you have any possessions and money, thank God for them, and do not compare yourself with others who are richer than you, but be content with what you have, and do not grieve if you lose some money, because it is changeable, but let this be a motive for you to cling to the love of God, for it is the only firm foundation and the unshakable support.

19.15.0.en: After Christ spoke of the importance of giving up the love of money so that a person may follow Him, Peter wanted to be assured for himself and the disciples, what would be their reward, since they had forsaken all for His sake? And what is meant is not only leaving the nets and possessions, because they are small, but even more the enduring of weariness and opposition from the Pharisees.

19.15.1.en: And the words of Peter may carry a kind of weakness of faith, so that he needs assurance of the reward from Christ, and may also carry a kind of feeling in himself that he has given. But he will discover after the accomplishment of redemption that everything a person gives is nothing before the perfect love in the giving of Christ Himself on the cross for the salvation of mankind.

19.16.0.en: Christ declared a great reward for His disciples who followed Him, indeed for everyone who follows Him, that in the regeneration, when the image of Christ changes from the weak human appearance to God the Judge in the Kingdom, His followers will be beside Him with a great standing, as proved by His saying: you shall sit upon thrones to judge the world, and this is by the faith of His followers and their preaching in His name, they judge the Jews who refused to believe, although they should have been the first to receive Him.

19.17.0.en: Christ affirmed the reward of the detached, and of one who gives up his attachment to possessions or loved ones in order to consecrate his heart to the love and service of God, which is that he receives a hundredfold in this life. And what is meant is not material compensation, but rather peace and love.

19.17.1.en: For example, the monk who leaves a father or mother and does not marry and beget children for the sake of God, God makes all people brothers and loved ones to him, and God becomes a father to him who cares for him and compensates him for all fatherhood of the flesh, and all become his children, and he finds his material sufficiency, and more than that. And some monks are chosen to become bishops, and all the money and possessions of the Church are placed under their hands, and they direct them with wisdom. Then what is better than that, the eternal reward in the Kingdom, which cannot be expressed.

19.17.2.en: God cannot be indebted to anyone, so what a person gives up, He will compensate him for in the present life, meeting the needs of His children, and then reward them with the greatest thing, which is the Kingdom of Heaven. And this is a clear truth that we observe, that those who love God and give up material things, He gives them favor in the eyes of all, and they are loved by many.

19.18.0.en: And so we find many great people in the world whose place in heaven is behind others, or who have no place in the Kingdom. And on the contrary, many of the despised and the least in the sight of men become great in the Kingdom of Heaven, such as the saints who renounced the world and lived in the wilderness, or the martyrs who endured many tortures. And likewise the first in their own eyes, that is, the proud, are preceded by the humble, that is, the last in their own eyes.

19.18.1.en: And there is another meaning, that those who were called first, like the Jews, may be rejected if they do not believe in Christ, and the Gentiles who were called after them and believed will have an advanced place in heaven.

19.18.2.en: Be confident that everything you leave on earth, you will receive in exchange for it peace and joy on earth, and manifold more in heaven. So do not be troubled if you lose something for the sake of Christ, or give up something to gain the love of others for the salvation of their souls. And on the contrary, you are the wiser the more you are able to give in this life, because this is a declaration of your love for Christ.

19.18.3.en: The parable of the laborers, seeking chief place
